# Glossary

## A

### Abstraction {#gls-abstraction}

In programming, an abstraction represents a common idea or operation while
leaving out details that are not essential to using it. A useful abstraction
groups code that performs the same conceptual task and can therefore be used
through a common interface.

Similar-looking code does not necessarily belong to the same abstraction. The
important question is whether the code has the same purpose and responsibility.
In MiniFEM, for example, matrix assembly can be shared because the same
local-to-global scatter-add operation is used for different element
formulations, while the element stiffness calculations remain specific to each
formulation.

**Further details:** [Wikipedia --- Abstraction (computer
science)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abstraction_(computer_science)).

### Affine mapping {#gls-affine-mapping}

A one-dimensional coordinate transformation of the form

$$
  x(\xi)=a_0+a_1\xi,
$$

which combines a constant scaling with a translation. For a two-node bar element
extending from $x_1$ to $x_2>x_1$, the affine mapping from the standard interval
$\xi\in[-1,1]$ to the physical element is

$$
  x(\xi)
  =
  \frac{1-\xi}{2}x_1
  +
  \frac{1+\xi}{2}x_2
  =
  \frac{x_1+x_2}{2}
  +
  \frac{L_e}{2}\xi,
$$

where $L_e=x_2-x_1>0$. This mapping sends $\xi=-1$ to $x_1$ and $\xi=1$ to
$x_2$. Its Jacobian is constant and equal to

$$
  J=\frac{dx}{d\xi}=\frac{L_e}{2}.
$$

The mapping and its Jacobian belong to an exact change of coordinate, as
developed in @sec-standard-physical-coordinates. Numerical approximation begins
only when a quadrature rule is subsequently applied to the transformed integral.

### Asymptotic behavior {#gls-asymptotic-behavior}

The behavior of a quantity as a parameter approaches a limiting value. An
asymptotic statement describes what happens near that limit; it does not
generally claim that the stated relationship is an exact equality for every
value of the parameter.

In numerical integration, for example,

$$
  e_Q(h)=O(h^2)
$$

as $h$ approaches zero means that there are constants $C>0$ and $h_0>0$,
independent of $h$, such that

$$
  e_Q(h)\leq Ch^2
$$

whenever $0<h\leq h_0$. Thus, once the subinterval width is sufficiently small,
the error is bounded above by a constant times $h^2$.

The big-$O$ statement specifies this asymptotic bound; it does not by itself
claim that

$$
  e_Q(h)=Ch^2
$$

or prescribe an exact error-reduction factor. If, more specifically, the error
approaches a nonzero multiple of $h^2$, halving $h$ reduces the error by
approximately a factor of four once the asymptotic behavior has been reached.

On a fixed integration interval divided into $n$ equal subintervals,

$$
  h=\frac{b-a}{n},
$$

so the same asymptotic bound may be written as

$$
  e_Q=O(n^{-2})
$$

as $n$ increases.

The quadratic midpoint-rule example in @sec-numerical-integration-one-dimension
is stronger than this general asymptotic statement. For that particular function
and interval, its error satisfies the exact relationship

$$
  e_Q=\frac{h^2}{4}
$$

for every positive integer $n$. Consequently, doubling $n$ and therefore halving
$h$ reduces the error by exactly a factor of four in that example.

## C

### Cohesion {#gls-cohesion}

The degree to which the responsibilities within a function, module, or file
belong together. High cohesion means that the contained operations serve a
clear, closely related purpose. For example, the local-to-global matrix and
vector assembly operations in MiniFEM form a small, cohesive family because they
both add element contributions to global finite element arrays, as illustrated
by the S06 refactoring in @sec-shared-fem-assembly.

**Further details:** [Wikipedia --- Cohesion (computer
science)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cohesion_%28computer_science%29).

### Coupling {#gls-coupling}

The degree to which one part of a program depends on details of another part.
Lower coupling is often useful because a function can then change independently
of details that are outside its responsibility. For example, a local-to-global
assembly operation needs a local contribution and a DOF map, but does not need
to know how a spring or bar formulation produced that contribution.

**Further details:** [Wikipedia --- Coupling (computer
programming)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupling_%28computer_programming%29).

## D

### Declarative programming {#gls-declarative-programming}

A programming paradigm in which the desired result is specified without
explicitly prescribing the sequence of operations required to obtain it. In
other words, declarative programming focuses on **what** should be achieved,
while the underlying implementation determines **how** to achieve it. For
example, selecting all even values from an array using a filtering operation
expresses the desired result without explicitly defining the iteration and state
changes required to construct it.

**See also:** [Imperative programming](#gls-imperative-programming). **Further
details:** [Wikipedia --- Declarative
programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Declarative_programming).

### Don't Repeat Yourself (DRY) {#gls-dry}

A design principle that encourages a stable piece of knowledge or responsibility
to have one well-defined implementation. It is not an absolute prohibition on
duplicated syntax: repeated code should be abstracted when it represents the
same stable responsibility and the resulting abstraction improves the design.
MiniFEM, for example, retains element-specific formulation code while sharing
the local-to-global assembly operation, as illustrated by the S06 refactoring in
@sec-shared-fem-assembly.

**Further details:** [Wikipedia --- Don't repeat
yourself](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don%27t_repeat_yourself).

## I

### Immutable object {#gls-immutable-object}

An object whose contents or internal state cannot be changed after it has been
created. An operation that appears to modify an immutable object instead creates
a new object representing the modified value, leaving the original object
unchanged. Strings and numbers are common examples of immutable objects in many
programming languages.

**See also:** [Mutable object](#gls-mutable-object); [Modified in
place](#gls-modified-in-place).

### Imperative programming {#gls-imperative-programming}

A programming paradigm in which a computation is expressed as an explicit
sequence of commands that describe **how** a result should be obtained.
Imperative programs typically modify variables or other aspects of the program
state as execution proceeds. For example, selecting all even values from an
array by iterating through its elements, testing each value, and adding the
matching values to a new array follows an imperative approach.

**See also:** [Declarative programming](#gls-declarative-programming). **Further
details:** [Wikipedia --- Imperative
programming](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Imperative_programming).

## M

### Modified in place {#gls-modified-in-place}

Describes an operation that changes an existing object or data structure
directly, rather than creating and returning a separate modified copy.

For example, in Julia, integers are immutable:

```julia
x = 4
x = x + 1
```

Here, `x` is not modified in place. Instead, `x` is rebound from the value `4`
to the new value `5`.

By contrast, an array is mutable:

```julia
x = [4]
x[1] += 1
```

Here, the existing array is modified in place, changing its contents from `[4]`
to `[5]`.

**See also:** [Mutable object](#gls-mutable-object); [Immutable
object](#gls-immutable-object).

### Mutable object {#gls-mutable-object}

An object whose contents or internal state can be changed after it has been
created. Operations on a mutable object may therefore modify the existing object
directly rather than creating a new one. Lists and dictionaries are common
examples of mutable objects in many programming languages.

**See also:** [Immutable object](#gls-immutable-object); [Modified in
place](#gls-modified-in-place).

## R

### Refactoring {#gls-refactoring}

Restructuring existing code to improve its organization, readability, or reuse
while preserving its intended computational behavior.

### Regression test {#gls-regression-test}

An automated test that checks whether previously accepted behavior remains
unchanged after modifications to the code. A regression test compares current
results with established reference values or properties so that unintended
changes can be detected.

In MiniFEM, regression tests may protect previously verified displacements,
reactions, element quantities, quadrature properties, or other numerical results
while new functionality is introduced. They support verification of later code
changes, but they do not replace independent analytical verification or physical
validation.

## S

### Separation of concerns {#gls-separation-of-concerns}

A software-design principle in which different aspects of a program are kept in
distinct parts of the code so that each part addresses a specific concern. For
example, a numerical function can perform a finite element operation while
diagnostic output is handled separately.

**Further details:** [Wikipedia --- Separation of
concerns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_concerns).

### Single Responsibility Principle {#gls-single-responsibility-principle}

A design principle stating that a function, module, or other program component
should have a coherent responsibility and a principal reason to change. It does
not mean that every component must perform only one small action. For example,
element-response recovery may coherently compute several related physical
quantities, while element formulation and local-to-global assembly have
different reasons to change and can be separated, as illustrated by the S06
refactoring in @sec-shared-fem-assembly.

**Further details:** [Wikipedia --- Single-responsibility
principle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Single-responsibility_principle).
